title: How Do Banks and Insurers Analyze Customer Feedback at Scale?
summary: Banks and insurers analyze customer feedback at scale with an operating model: one taxonomy, impact ranking, root cause and an owning team per theme.
body_markdown:
Banks, lenders and insurers hear from customers everywhere. Net promoter score (NPS) and customer satisfaction (CSAT) surveys, complaints, contact-center notes, app store reviews and review sites all carry the same problems in different words. The volume keeps rising. The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) received[more than 6.6 million consumer complaints in 2025](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/2025-consumer-response-annual-report/) , up from nearly 3.2 million in 2024. Most of that signal sits in separate systems owned by separate teams. Nobody sees the whole picture.


Banks and insurers that analyze customer feedback at scale run it as an operating model, not a reporting task. They pull every channel into one place, theme it with one consistent taxonomy, rank themes by their impact on a business score, assign each theme to the team that owns the fix, and track whether the fix worked. Thematic is a customer feedback analytics platform built for that model. It themes feedback from surveys, support tickets, call center transcripts, app reviews and CRM notes. It scores each theme by business impact. And it traces every theme back to the exact comments behind it.


Below are the six steps, a worked example from a large financial services provider, and the mistakes that stall most programs.


## The six-step process


1. **Consolidate every channel.** Bring surveys, complaints, contact-center notes and reviews into one dataset.
2. **Build one taxonomy across channels.** Use the same themes for a complaint and a survey comment about the same issue.
3. **Rank themes by impact, not volume.** Measure which themes move NPS, CSAT or complaint rates.
4. **Find the root cause behind each theme.** Drill from broad themes to the specific sub-theme that explains them.
5. **Map each theme to an owning team.** Give every driver a named owner who can fix it.
6. **Close the loop and evidence the outcome.** Route actions, check the score moved, and keep the record.


## Step 1: Consolidate every channel


Each channel shows a different slice of the customer experience. Surveys capture people who chose to respond. Complaints capture people angry enough to escalate. Contact-center notes capture the problems customers called about. App reviews capture what digital customers say in public.


Regulators expect firms to look across sources. In its[2024 review of outcomes monitoring at insurers](https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/multi-firm-reviews/insurance-multi-firm-review-outcomes-monitoring-under-consumer-duty) , the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) criticized firms "highly reliant on net promoter scores" and noted that "Focusing too much on complaints pushes responsibility on to customers." It praised the opposite pattern: "More developed approaches were able to show a wide range of sources."


At scale,[consolidation](https://getthematic.com/insights/integrate-feedback-sources-analytics-platform) is a volume problem as well as a coverage problem. A[US online lending marketplace](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-feedback-analytics-financial-services-use-cases) using Thematic processes over 20,000 customer comments every 90 days across 10 data sources spanning 7 product verticals. Manual coding can't keep up with that.


**Common mistake:** analyzing each channel in its own tool, then trying to reconcile the reports in a slide deck.


## Step 2: Build one taxonomy across channels


A single taxonomy means "unclear fee disclosure" is the same theme whether it arrives as a complaint, a survey verbatim or a one-star app review. Without it, the complaints team and the customer experience (CX) team count the same problem twice under different names. Then they argue about which number is right.


The taxonomy also has to stay consistent month to month. If themes shift every time someone reruns the analysis, trend lines become meaningless.


Thematic builds themes bottom-up from the language customers actually use, not from a predefined list. It organizes them into broad categories and sub-themes, and analysts refine the theme set into a compact, tuned taxonomy so the monthly read stays comparable.


## Step 3: Rank themes by impact, not volume


The[most-mentioned issue](https://getthematic.com/insights/most-common-complaints-arent-biggest-problems) is rarely the most damaging one. A theme that appears in a small share of comments can drag a score down more than a theme everyone mentions in passing.


[Impact analysis](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) compares the score of customers who mention a theme against the overall score. Thematic's score-change waterfall shows which themes moved NPS between two periods, and by how many points. That turns a monthly score into a ranked list of what to fix.


**Common mistake:** prioritizing by complaint count. Volume tells you what is loud. Impact tells you what is costly.


## Step 4: Find the root cause behind each theme


"Mortgage application" is a theme. "Customers calling because they don't know why their mortgage request wasn't accepted" is a root cause. Teams can act on the second one.


The FCA's[guidance on complaints and root cause analysis](https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/good-and-poor-practice/complaints-and-root-cause-analysis-good-practice-and-areas-improvement) asks firms to "identify the root causes of systemic or recurring problems." In practice, that means drilling from category to sub-theme to the underlying comments.


Thematic supports that drill-down. Its themes run from broad categories to sub-themes, and every theme traces back to the exact comments behind it.


Thematic also[flags emerging issues early](https://getthematic.com/insights/identify-root-causes-support-tickets-automatically) , at around a 0.5% mention rate, so teams catch new root causes before they show up in complaint volumes.


## Step 5: Map each theme to an owning team


This is the step most programs skip, and the one that decides whether anything changes. An insight without an owner is a slide. An insight with an owner is a work item.


The FCA's root cause analysis review makes the same point: good practice means "the person who owns the process, system, communication or customer journey is involved." For a bank or insurer, that means a clear map from theme to function. An illustrative version:


**Theme family** **Typical owning team** **Example signal**


Statements, letters, notices Client communications Confusing wording in survey verbatims


Wait times, call handling Contact center operations Repeat-contact themes in call notes


App login, payments, errors Digital product One-star app store reviews


Fees, pricing, rates Product and pricing Fee themes in complaints and NPS detractors


Claims or applications Operations Status-update themes across channels


Once the map exists, every function can see its own contribution to the score. Thematic's Workflows send automated email or Slack alerts to the teams that own each theme, for example when a theme spikes or new comments match a filter.


## Step 6: Close the loop and evidence the outcome


[Closing the loop](https://getthematic.com/insights/close-the-customer-feedback-loop) has two halves. The inner loop is making things right for an individual customer. The outer loop is fixing the underlying issue so it stops happening. At scale, the outer loop is where the value sits.


Evidence is the part regulators find missing. In the same insurance review, the FCA found that "Few firms were able to provide clear evidence of where the monitoring of outcomes had directly led to proactive action." Its complaints guidance highlights firms that "checked whether the change had addressed the problem."


The fix is to rerun the same impact analysis after each change. If the owning team fixed the root cause, the theme's drag on the score should shrink in the next period. Thematic's[Actions Agent](https://getthematic.com/insights/actions-agent-closing-loop-customer-intelligence) , currently in early access through Thematic Next, recommends next-best actions for each piece of feedback.


## A worked example: a large financial services provider


A[large financial services provider](https://getthematic.com/case-studies/financial-services) ran an independent competitive NPS survey with under a hundred responses a month. The score was negative, and the monthly read reported the number without explaining it.


The insights team used Thematic's score-change waterfall to quantify which themes moved NPS. They then mapped each theme to the department that owned it, so each function could see its own contribution to the score.


The results:


- NPS moved from negative to positive, a rise of more than 20 points.
- The CX and contact team was the single largest departmental contributor, at roughly 8 points.
- Client communications contributed roughly 7 points.
- Fees were a modest drag, and the one area where the provider trailed peers.


The business simplified its client communications and coached frontline teams. As the case study puts it, "The monthly read moved from a number to a diagnosis."


The lesson is not the volume. It is the ownership map. Once each driver had an owner, each owner had a number to move.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Relying on one data source.** NPS alone or complaints alone gives a partial view. Combine surveys, complaints, contact-center notes and reviews.
- **Counting instead of weighing.** Rank themes by score impact, not by mention count.
- **Rebuilding the taxonomy every quarter.** Keep a consistent theme set so trends hold.
- **Stopping at the dashboard.** Assign every high-impact theme to a named owning team.
- **Not checking the fix.** Rerun impact analysis after each change and keep the evidence.
- **Hiding the comments.** Every theme should trace back to the verbatims behind it, so owners trust the finding.


## The short answer


Banks and insurers analyze customer feedback at scale by treating it as an operating model: consolidate every channel, theme it consistently, rank themes by impact, find root causes, assign each to an owning team, and evidence the result.
